abstract: Squelching is an indirect inhibition of transcription that results from redistribution of cofactors away from DNA. Here, we describe a class of Lis homology (LisH)-derived peptides that act as transcriptional squelchers. LisH domains are a highly conserved motif found in 10s of thousands of proteins and are composed of ~30 amino acids in a helix-turn-helix fold. By examining a phylogenetically diverse subset of LisH domains in a synthetic Saccharomyces cerevisiae assay, we identified a small number of hydrophobic residues within the first helix that are required for effective inhibition of reporter expression. In addition, squelching required binding to the general transcriptional cofactor Taf5, a subunit of the TFIID complex. Transcriptome-level impacts were largely correlated in yeast expressing two distinct LisH sequences, consistent with a model that LisH-based squelching results from a shared mechanism of sequestering Taf5. Consistent with that inference, overexpression of Taf5 partially reversed the squelching effect. Given the interest in squelching as a potential area for anti-cancer therapies, we also tested whether our shortest squelching sequence called YC5C-H1 had any effect on the human colorectal cancer cell line HCT-15. In addition to preferentially squelching high expression genes, YC5C-H1 sharply slowed growth of HCT-15 cells.
